facts.statement: Baryonyx lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: Baryonyx () is a genus of theropod dinosaur which lived in the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous period, about 130–125 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first skeleton of Baryonyx was discovered in 1983 in the Smokejack Clay Pit in Surrey, England.
facts.quote: The first skeleton was discovered in 1983 in the Smokejack Clay Pit, of Surrey, England, in sediments of the Weald Clay Formation

facts.statement: Baryonyx was named by palaeontologists Alan J. Charig and Angela C. Milner in 1986.
facts.quote: named by palaeontologists Alan J. Charig and Angela C. Milner in 1986

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Baryonyx was estimated to be between 7.5 and 10 meters long and weigh between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, which may not have been fully grown, was estimated to have been between 7.5 and 10 m long and to have weighed between 1.2 and 2 MT.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had robust forelimbs with a first-finger claw measuring approximately 31 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: It had robust forelimbs, with the eponymous first-finger claw measuring about 31 cm long.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur proven to be piscivorous, based on fish scales found in the stomach region of the holotype.
facts.quote: Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur demonstrated to have been piscivorous (fish-eating), as evidenced by fish scales in the stomach region of the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Baryonyx may have had semi-aquatic habits.
facts.quote: Baryonyx may have had semi-aquatic habits

facts.statement: Baryonyx is classified as a member of the family Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: Now recognised as a member of the family Spinosauridae

facts.statement: Amateur fossil collector William J. Walker discovered the initial remains of Baryonyx in January 1983 at the Smokejack Clay Pit.
facts.quote: In January 1983, the plumber and amateur fossil collector William J. Walker explored the Smokejack Clay Pit

facts.statement: William J. Walker donated the claw to the Natural History Museum, while the Ockley Brick Company donated the rest of the skeleton and equipment.
facts.quote: Walker donated the claw to the museum, and the Ockley Brick Company (owners of the pit) donated the rest of the skeleton and provided equipment.

facts.statement: It took six years of constant preparation to extract all the bones from the rock matrix of the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: It took six years of almost constant preparation to get all the bones out of the rock

facts.statement: The holotype specimen represents approximately 65 percent of the complete skeleton.
facts.quote: The specimen represents about 65 per cent of the skeleton

facts.statement: It is debated whether Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym of Baryonyx and whether Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus, with some researchers suggesting they are synonyms while others keep them separate.
facts.quote: Some researchers have suggested that Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym (being an older name), and that Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus; subsequent authors have kept them separate.

facts.statement: In 2019, Thomas M. S. Arden and colleagues concluded that a Portuguese skeleton previously attributed to Baryonyx did not belong to the genus because its dentary bone was not strongly upturned.
facts.quote: In 2019, the palaeontologist Thomas M. S. Arden and colleagues found that the Portuguese skeleton did not belong to Baryonyx, since the front of its dentary bone was not strongly upturned.

facts.statement: In 2024, Erik Isasmendi and colleagues concluded that no spinosaurid specimens from Iberia could be assigned to Baryonyx.
facts.quote: A 2024 article by the palaeontologist Erik Isasmendi and colleagues reviewed the spinosaurid fossil record of Iberia and concluded that no specimens from there could be assigned to Baryonyx.

facts.statement: In 2002, Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues proposed that Suchomimus tenerensis was a species of Baryonyx and that Suchomimus was identical to Cristatusaurus.
facts.quote: In 2002, the palaeontologist Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues proposed that Suchomimus tenerensis was similar enough to Baryonyx walkeri to be considered a species within the same genus (as B. tenerensis), and that Suchomimus was identical to Cristatusaurus.

facts.statement: In 2026, Frédéric Pittet suggested that shared features in Cristatusaurus and Suchomimus confirmed their synonymy, distinguishing them from Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 2026, the palaeontologist Frédéric Pittet found that assigned specimens of Cristatusaurus and Suchomimus shared features such as a crest on the premaxilla not found in Baryonyx, and suggested this confirmed the synonymy of the Nigerien taxa.

facts.statement: Baryonyx is estimated to have been between 7.5 and 10 meters long, 2.5 meters in hip height, and weighed between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
facts.quote: Baryonyx is estimated to have been between 7.5 and 10 m long, 2.5 m in hip height, and to have weighed between 1.2 and 2 MT.

facts.statement: The fused sternum of the Baryonyx holotype specimen indicates that the individual may have been mature.
facts.quote: On the other hand, the specimen's fused sternum indicates that it may have been mature.

facts.statement: The skull of Baryonyx was estimated to be 91 to 95 cm long based on comparisons with the related genus Suchomimus.
facts.quote: The full length of the skull is estimated to have been 91 - 95 cm long, based on comparison with that of the related genus Suchomimus (which was 20% larger).

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone formed a solid, almost triangular horn core similar to those in Allosaurus, distinct from other spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The lacrimal bone in front of the eye appears to have formed a horn core similar to those seen, for example, in Allosaurus, and was distinct from other spinosaurids in being solid and almost triangular.

facts.statement: The neck of Baryonyx formed an S shape, though it was straighter than in other theropods.
facts.quote: Initially thought to have lacked the sigmoid curve typical of theropods, the neck of Baryonyx does appear to have formed an S shape, though straighter than in other theropods.

facts.statement: The coracoid connected with the scapula in a unique peg-and-notch articulation found only among spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The coracoid tapered hind-wards when viewed in profile, and, uniquely among spinosaurids, connected with the scapula in a peg-and-notch articulation.

facts.statement: The humerus was short and stout with ends broadly expanded and flattened for muscle attachment and limb articulation.
facts.quote: The humerus was short and stout, with its ends broadly expanded and flattened—the upper side for the deltopectoral crest and muscle attachment and the lower for articulation with the radius and ulna.

facts.statement: Sereno and colleagues suggested that some cranial bones were misidentified by Charig and Milner, leading to an overly deep reconstruction of the occiput, and proposed the skull was actually as low, long, and narrow as that of Suchomimus.
facts.quote: Sereno and colleagues suggested that some of Baryonyx cranial bones had been misidentified by Charig and Milner, resulting in the occiput being reconstructed as too deep, and that the skull was instead probably as low, long and narrow as that of Suchomimus.

facts.statement: Baryonyx is classified within the family Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Spinosauridae

facts.statement: Baryonyx belongs to the subfamily Baryonychinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Baryonychinae

facts.statement: Baryonyx is part of the superfamily Megalosauroidea.
facts.quote: superfamilia: Megalosauroidea

facts.statement: Charig and Milner originally described Baryonyx as unique enough to warrant a new family, Baryonychidae.
facts.quote: In their original description, Charig and Milner found Baryonyx unique enough to warrant a new family of theropod dinosaurs: Baryonychidae.

facts.statement: In 1990, Charig and Milner dismissed the idea that Baryonyx was related to spinosaurids because they did not find the remains similar enough.
facts.quote: In 1990, Charig and Milner dismissed the spinosaurid affinities of Baryonyx, since they did not find their remains similar enough.

facts.statement: Holtz and colleagues listed Baryonychidae as a synonym of Spinosauridae in 2004.
facts.quote: Holtz and colleagues listed Baryonychidae as a synonym of Spinosauridae in 2004.

facts.statement: Baryonyx lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 130 y 125 millones de años durante el Aptiense, en lo que es hoy Europa.

facts.statement: The first specimen of Baryonyx was found in England.
facts.quote: El primer ejemplar fue encontrado en Inglaterra.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was a large predator measuring approximately 9.75 meters in length, 2.55 meters in height at the hip, and weighing between 1.7 and 2.7 tons.
facts.quote: Baryonyx era un predador de gran tamaño que midió unos 9.75 metros de longitud, 2.55 de altura a la cadera y entre 1.7 y 2.7 toneladas

facts.statement: The skull and vertebral elements of the holotype specimen NHM R9951 do not appear fused, suggesting the individual was not fully grown.
facts.quote: El hecho que los elementos del cráneo y la columna vertebral del espécimen holotipo de B. walkeri, NHM R9951, no parecen haber estado fusionados, lo que sugiere que el individuo no estaba completamente crecido

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a pair of large curved claws about 35 centimeters long located on its hands rather than its feet.
facts.quote: Baryonyx tenía un par de grandes garras curvas, de alrededor de 35 centímetros, pero al contrario que éstos, no se situaba en los pies, sino en las manos.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a long neck that was very inflexible and did not have the S-shape seen in many other theropods.
facts.quote: El largo cuello era muy poco flexible y no tenía la forma en S de muchos otros terópodos.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had large jaws that were uniquely crocodilian in appearance and contained 96 teeth, double the number of most of its relatives.
facts.quote: Las grandes mandíbulas eran singularmente cocodrilianas en aspecto y tenían 96 dientes, el doble que la mayoría de sus parientes.

facts.statement: Researchers considered the possibility that Baryonyx was a thecodont due to apparently primitive features, though this grouping is now considered unnatural.
facts.quote: They found Baryonyx to be unlike any other theropod group, and considered the possibility that it was a thecodont (a grouping of early archosaurs now considered unnatural), due to having apparently primitive features

facts.statement: In 2010, Roger Benson considered the clade Spinosauroidea a junior synonym of Megalosauroidea.
facts.quote: In 2010, the palaeontologist Roger Benson considered this a junior synonym of Megalosauroidea (an older name).

facts.statement: Denver W. Fowler suggested in 2007 that clade names like Spinosauroidea and Baryonychinae should be replaced by names based on Suchosaurus.
facts.quote: In a 2007 conference abstract, the palaeontologist Denver W. Fowler suggested that since Suchosaurus is the first named genus in its group, the clade names Spinosauroidea, Spinosauridae, and Baryonychinae should be replaced by Suchosauroidea, Suchosauridae, and Suchosaurinae

facts.statement: The estimated total length of the Baryonyx skull is 950 millimeters, based on comparisons with the related genus Suchomimus.
